summary: Only response_C correctly identifies 15 as the minimum number of inspections with valid upper bound proof (1 inspection from 'Mixed' envelope + 14 to distinguish pure from 7/13 mixed) and valid lower bound reasoning (need 14 to beat 13 majority sequences). Response_G has structurally correct reasoning but miscounts by 1 (says 16). All other responses suffer from invalid one-draw inferences (A, D, F, H), contradictory oscillation (E), or incomplete strategy synthesis (B).
cross_response_observations: Multiple responses (A, D, F, H) share the common defect of invalid one-draw inference - claiming that observing one sequence from an envelope proves that envelope's type, ignoring that the mixed envelope can return its majority type (up to 13 sequences) and thus match a pure envelope's first observation. Responses A, D, and H all claim that 1-4 inspections suffice by treating single observations as definitive, while F claims 3 inspections suffice with the same flawed logic. Response_E exhibits unique oscillation behavior, cycling through multiple incompatible answers (2, 3, 14, 15) without ever committing to coherent reasoning. Response_B provides partial strategy description but fails to specify concrete branch-by-branch label-fixing rules, ending with hand-wavy synthesis. Response_G stands out as having structurally correct worst-case reasoning but miscounts the total (16 instead of 15), possibly due to double-counting the initial inspection. Only response_C correctly identifies that 14 inspections are needed after the first to distinguish pure from mixed (since mixed has at most 13 of any type), giving the correct total of 15. The pattern of ignoring the 7/13 split in the mixed envelope is widespread - most responses fail to recognize that 13 sequences of one type in the mixed envelope creates the need for 14 inspections to guarantee distinguishing pure from mixed.
